5 of the Rarest American High-Performance Road Cars From the 1960s
16 photos
Photo: RM Sotheby's
The 1960s saw American carmakers unleash a long list of raw high-performance versions of their production models. But while most were produced in large numbers, some were build in extremely low figures, making them iconic holy grails.
In more ways than one, the 1960s was a transformative decade in American history. From the civil rights movement to landing on the moon, that period was marked by huge leaps for society.
For the local automotive industry, the 1960s marked the beginning of a short yet memorable era of untamed performance.
Whether on the world’s most legendary race tracks, local drag strips, an empty stretches of public roads, American cars were setting new standards for factory-built performance.
The decade saw the introduction of many impressive high-performance machines built in the US. But while some sold in huge numbers, some special-order brutes quietly earned their place in automotive history books with their impressive performance prowess and rarity.
1963 Pontiac Catalina 421 Super Duty – 14 units Photo: Mecum Auctions Pontiac is widely credited with kickstarting the muscle car craze in 1964, when it added the GTO package to the intermediate Tempest/LeMans line.
However, a year before that legendary muscle car was born, the GM division introduced a special-order, drag-strip-oriented beast that packed a whole lot of muscle into a full-size chassis.
That beast was none other than the 1963 Pontiac Catalina 421 Super Duty, an ultra-rare performance icon that earned the nickname Swiss Cheese ."
Photo: Mecum Auctions That name came from the fac that each of the fourteen units built was put on an extensive weight-saving diet which, apart from the removal of features such as carpeting and sound insulation, included over 100 large holes being punched into the frame rails.
The epic full-size coupe was powered by a race-bred, 421-ci (6.9-liter) Super Duty V8 that Pontiac rated at 405 hp. However, the engine was allegedly capable of close to 500 hp.
Theoretically street legal, the 1963 Pontiac Catalina 421 Super Duty was one of the most insane drag-strip specials produced during the golden age of muscle.
1966 Dodge Coronet HEMI Sedan – 5 units Photo: Mecum Auctions The Chrysler Corporation introduced the now-legendary 426 HEMI V8 in 1964 as a competition-only motor conceived to give the Plymouth and Dodge brands the edge in NASCAR.
However, the competition’s governing body modified the rulebook a year later, forcing the corporation to develop a street version of the engine and make it available in its production models.
That led Plymouth and Dodge to add the 426 street HEMI as an option for many of its cars for the 1966 model year.
Photo: Mecum Auctions While most enthusiasts added the HEMI option to a two-door coupe, a very few decided to add the Elephant engine to the Coronet sedan.
The exact number of HEMI-powered Coronet sedans produced in 1966 was five, all of which delivered with the upscale Deluxe trim.
One of the rarest, most intriguing American performance models of the 1960s, the Coronet HEMI sedan looked just like a conventional Coronet Deluxe, but with 425-hp on tap, it became one of the most impressive factory-built sleepers ever produced.
1966 Shelby GT350 Convertible – 4 units Photo: Mecum Auctions For 1965, the first full model year for the Mustang, which was introduced halfway through the 1964 model year, Ford partnered up with Carroll Shelby and his Shelby American crew to transform the model into a genuine performance car.
The result was the Shelby GT350 , a tuned, lightweight variant of the Mustang fastback coupe which immediately proved its worth on the street and the track.
For the 1966 model year, the GT350 returned with several improvements but the story goes that one particular buyer wanted Shelby to add a convertible option to that list of improvements.
Photo: Mecum Auctions That buyer was Bob Shane, a member of the pop group “ The Kingston Trio ,” who was close friends with Carroll Shelby and managed to convince the engineering mastermind to build a drop-top GT350.
Despite the fact that Shelby didn’t initially consider building a convertible version due to chassis rigidity concerns, he went on to build one for Shane anyway, then put together three more to see if how fast he could sell them.
While based on the standard ragtop Mustang, the 1966 GT350 convertible featured all the modifications of its fixed-roof sibling. That meant a tweaked suspension and a 306-hp HiPo K-Code version of the Windsor 289 nestled between its shock towers.
Shelby managed to sell the additional convertibles quite fast, but decided against offering one for the 1967 model year. However, a convertible GT350 finally arrived a year later and was produced in 404 examples.
1967 Dodge Coronet R/T HEMI Convertible – 3 units Photo: Mecum Auctions Dodge and Plymouth continued to offer the Elephant engine for the 1967 model year, but by now, the engine was only available on select two-door models.
The vast majority of buyers who ticked the HEMI option on the ordered sheet purchased a hardtop because the chassis was more rigid than the convertible.
Nevertheless, a few drop-top enthusiasts chose to equip their new rides with the 425-hp Elephant engine.
Photo: Mecum Auctions Of the ragtops sold in 1967 with a HEMI under the hood , the rarest was the Coronet R/T, of which Dodge produced just three units.
Two of them were equipped with a four-speed manual gearbox, while a single one received the 426 HEMI/three-speed Torqueflite automatic powertrain combo.
Today all three 1967 Coronet R/T HEMI Convertibles survive and are considered some of the most sought-after muscle cars ever produced.
1969 Chevrolet Corvette ZL1 – 2 units Photo: RM Sotheby's While GM had a strict ban on motorsport during the latter part of the 1960s, for the 1969 model year, several important Chevy dealers devised a clever scheme to build some uniquely impressive rides through the COPO (Central Office Production Order) fleet-ordering system.
The scheme led to the creation of several Camaros equipped with the L72 427 big-block V8 and the race-bred, all-aluminum ZL1 version .
This resulted in 69 ZL1-equipped Camaros, 50 of which were delivered to Illinois-based Chevy dealer Fred Gibb, while the rest were distributed to other established dealerships throughout the country.
Photo: RM Sotheby's However, apart from the 69 Camaros, Chevy also built two special-order COPO Corvettes equipped with the legendary ZL1.
Rated at only 430 hp on paper, for insurance-related reasons, the aluminum ZL1 engine was actually capable of delivering well over 550 hp when put on a dyno.
With that engine under the hood, the Corvette could run the quarter mile in the low 12-second range in otherwise stock guise.
Today, the ZL1 remains the rarest factory-built Corvette and the two units are some of the most valuable examples of Chevy’s iconic sports car. Three years ago, the orange convertible shown above was auctioned off by RM Sotheby’s, fetching a jaw-dropping $3,140,000.
